title: Distributed Rate Limiter
subtitle: Token Bucket, Sliding Window Log & atomic Redis Lua enforcement
overview: Rate limiters protect downstream databases and GPU clusters from abuse, noisy neighbors, and cascading traffic spikes. In distributed fleets, local in-memory counters drift across nodes—requiring atomic Redis Lua scripts (Token Bucket or Sliding Window Counter) paired with explicit fail-open vs fail-closed policies.
firstPrinciplesStory: A single misconfigured partner retry script wakes up at 3 AM firing 10,000 POST /checkout calls per second. Your API pods auto-scale eagerly, which only multiplies the thundering wave hitting your single Postgres Primary until connection pools exhaust and paying customers get 503s. Putting a fixed-window counter in app memory fails because 20 gateway pods don't share state—and a naive Redis GET+SET races under concurrency. Thus you need atomic central accounting plus graceful failure boundaries.

adaptiveLenses.intuition: A Token Bucket is a coffee punch card that automatically adds 10 punches per second up to a max of 20. Short legitimate bursts spend saved punches smoothly, while sustained spam hits empty and politely gets told 'come back in 1 second' (HTTP 429).
adaptiveLenses.mechanics: Gateways execute an atomic `EVALSHA` Lua script on Redis that reads `(tokens, last_ts)`, refills proportional to `now - last_ts`, checks `tokens >= cost`, and decrements in one single-threaded operation (~0.6ms). Headers (`X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `Retry-After`) guide client backoff.
adaptiveLenses.staffTradeoffs: Redis round-trips on every request add ~0.6–1.5ms and risk turning Redis into a critical outage choke point. Staff engineers add local fast-reject caches for already-throttled keys, batch/sync quotas for ultra-high QPS, and explicit fail-open local caps for revenue endpoints vs fail-closed for security endpoints.

ddiaAnchors.concept: Why Time Calculations Belong Inside One Authoritative Clock
ddiaAnchors.whyItMatters: Using Redis `TIME` or single-node Lua timestamps avoids gateway clock skew across 50 API pods.

pragmaticTips.tip: Reject abusive traffic at the outermost gateway edge before wasting downstream CPU, auth joins, or DB connections.
pragmaticTips.application: Attach clear Retry-After headers + fail-open circuit breaker around Redis itself.

keyTakeaways: Token Bucket permits controlled bursts up to bucket capacity while enforcing a steady refill rate.
Executing read-compute-write inside a single Redis Lua script eliminates race conditions without distributed locks.
Return HTTP 429 with X-RateLimit-Remaining and Retry-After headers so well-behaved clients back off.

nodes.label: API Caller
nodes.summary: Mobile or B2B client hitting rate-limited REST endpoints.
failureModes: Aggressive retry loops without Retry-After jitter

nodes.label: API Gateway Fleet
nodes.summary: Extracts tenant/IP key, applies local fast-reject cache if already throttled, and queries Redis atomically.
whenToUse: Centralized edge throttling before auth-heavy or DB-heavy services
failureModes: Blocking request threads synchronously if Redis connection pool stalls

nodes.label: Redis Cluster (Lua)
nodes.summary: Stores `(tokens, last_refill_ts)` per key and runs atomic Lua token-bucket transitions in <1ms.
whenToUse: Shared global rate limits across stateless gateway instances
failureModes: Single hot tenant key hammering one Redis shard

nodes.label: Core Orders Service
nodes.summary: Downstream business service shielded from burst overload.
whenToUse: Expensive write paths, LLM inference, payment APIs
failureModes: Exhausts DB connections if unthrottled bursts leak through

steps.payloadInspector: Rate Key: rl:checkout:user_8841 | Rule: capacity=20, refill=10/sec
steps.inspectorNote: Gateway extracts user ID from verified JWT (or IP for anonymous routes) to construct the Redis key.

steps.info: EVALSHA refills +8 tokens, decrements 1 -> ALLOWED (14 remaining)
steps.payloadInspector: HMGET rl:checkout:user_8841 tokens ts -> refill(elapsed=0.8s) -> tokens=14 -> return {1, 14}
steps.inspectorNote: Because Redis runs Lua scripts single-threadedly, concurrent requests across 50 gateway pods cannot double-spend the last token.

predictPrompt.prompt: Why does implementing Token Bucket as `GET tokens` followed by `DECRBY` in Python/Go fail under concurrent gateway pods?
predictPrompt.hint: Two gateways read `tokens = 1` at the exact same millisecond.
predictPrompt.reveal: Check-then-act across separate network calls creates a classic race condition where multiple requests both observe `tokens = 1` and both pass. Putting the entire refill+check+decrement inside one Redis Lua script guarantees atomicity.

steps.inspectorNote: Rate limiter adds <1.5ms overhead while returning transparent quota telemetry headers.

chaosScenarios.title: Burst Exhaustion (HTTP 429) & Redis Timeout Fail-Open
chaosScenarios.triggerSummary: Bot script fires 250 req/sec, draining bucket to 0; subsequently Redis experiences a 50ms network blip.
chaosScenarios.mitigationSummary: Burst traffic receives immediate HTTP 429 + Retry-After; during Redis timeout, gateway switches to local fallback counter (fail-open) so legitimate users aren't blocked.

steps.payloadInspector:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 1
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
steps.inspectorNote: Gateway caches blocked flag locally for 100ms so subsequent bot spam doesn't even hit Redis.

steps.info: Redis timed out (>5ms) -> Gateway applies local emergency cap & fails open
steps.payloadInspector: CircuitBreaker: redis-rl OPEN -> using in-process per-pod soft limit
steps.inspectorNote: For revenue APIs, fail-open with a conservative in-memory pod cap prevents a Redis outage from taking down checkout.

cons: Needs tuning of both burst size and steady refill rate
tradeoffs.bestFor: General API gateways and user-facing quotas

pros: Eliminates boundary burst spikes seen in Fixed Window
cons: Log stores every timestamp (high RAM); Counter approximates previous window
